title: The art and science of facial reconstruction: a history

paragraphs.text: A century or so ago the discovery of ancient human bones was of relatively little importance to the archaeologist. While the opening up of a tomb full of gold and jewels could attract the attention of a wealthy patron, old bones held no such appeal. They were often piled into a cardboard box, stored deep in some dusty museum basement and all but forgotten — and some have been lost for ever. Even the Egyptian pharaoh Tutankhamun’s mummified body, once stripped of its gems and golden amulets, received less attention than most of the objects found in his tomb.

Today all this has been changed by recently developed techniques that enable an ancient skull, even one in a seriously fragmentary state, to be transformed into a vivid, accurate reconstruction of its owner’s face. And this can be done with such efficiency that today it is difficult to credit until the science behind it is properly understood.

It was the German anatomist W. His who was the pioneer. Around 1895 he took the first proper measurements of a facial dissected depth. He was able to draw up a complete table of the average tissue depths at key points, so that, by modelling clay over a skull to the same depths, the face of the living could be recreated. When His demonstrated this using a skull thought to be that of the seventeenth-century German composer Johann Sebastian Bach, the reconstruction received worldwide acclaim as a convincing representation. Bach’s known portraits of the composer. Soon His’s work was followed up and expanded on by the Swiss anatomist J. Kollman and his sculptor colleague W. Būchly, who produced a much more extensive set of tables for average tissue depths. Using these tables, they made the first truly scientific three-dimensional (3-D) facial reconstruction of a man from the Stone Age.

There followed a flurry of early twentieth-century reconstructions of pre-historic and historic skulls, all theoretically based on ‘scientific’ methods. However, it was observed that different sculptors were producing widely differing faces based on the same skull and data, and the method’s reliability was soon questioned.

Thankfully, a twentieth-century Russian palaeontologist, Mikhail Gerasimov, saved the method from being abandoned altogether. Gerasimov noted that paying particularly close attention to the musculature of the face and neck, as determined from the different points on the surviving bones, played an important part in achieving the best possible result. His method has since been further developed by Betty Pat Gatliff of Norman, Oklahoma. Now retired, Gatliff is noted for the 140 or so facial reconstructions that she has undertaken to help U.S. police in criminological cases, and which have contributed to some 105 positive identifications. Her historical reconstructions have been a spin-off from this work. A typical example of a Gatliff or ‘American’ reconstruction is the artist-anthropologist Sharon Long’s rendition of the face of a 9,400-year-old mummy – North America’s earliest example of mummification – found in 1940 in Spirit Cave near Fallon, Nevada.

Arguably a more advanced technique has been developed independently by Britain’s Richard Neave, now anatomical artist at the University of Manchester Medical School. After spending many years at art school, Neave went on to observe dissections being performed at hospitals in London and Manchester. While this gave him the necessary grounding for his subsequent career producing medical illustrations, he had little knowledge of his Russian and American counterparts’ work in facial reconstructions and initially relied on the Kollman and Būchly soft tissue thickness tables. He entered the field when the Manchester Museum Egyptologist Dr. Rosalie David asked him to reconstruct the faces of two ancient Egyptian mummies from the museum’s collection, the half-brothers Khnum-Nakht and Nekht-Ankh, who lived around 1900 B.C.

The know-how accompanying the various facial reconstruction methods has advanced quite spectacularly during the last three decades. For instance, ultrasound, which could be used on living subjects, now enables much more accurate measurements to be made of average tissue depths. The much greater volume of data thereby produced has led to widespread recognition that tissue depths can vary according to different facial types, and can also change as a result of gender. Another advance is that, whereas Neave was obliged to use X-rays of the facial bones when he worked on the facial reconstruction of a prehistoric man (the ‘Lindow Man’) in the 1980s, he can now use computer tomography (CT) scans. The disadvantage of X-rays is that, like conventional photographs, they are two-dimensional, so that any structures which they show appear superimposed on top of one another often making analysis problematic. In CT scans, however, the rays pass through at differing angles, thereby eliminating interference and enabling bone and other varieties of structure to be viewed selectively and in 3D.

Remarkably, CT scans can selectively ‘see’ through the bandages of ancient Egyptian mummies that have never been unwrapped, producing high-quality 3-D images of the body that, because the data is in digital form, can be fed to a computer. So when the living tissue data of a modern control face of the same type and bone structure are fed into the computer and digitally ‘morphed’ around the CT-scanned mummy skull, an on-screen reconstruction of the ancient face can be made. No one need ever have physically touched the original skull, or gained direct access to it.
